labelChirho: set sail, put out to sea
descriptionChirho: A nautical technical term meaning to put out from harbor, embark on a sea voyage, or set sail. Used almost exclusively in Acts for Paul's missionary journeys: Acts 13:13, 16:11, 18:21, 20:3,13, 21:1-2, 27:2,4,12,21, 28:10-11; also Luke 8:22 for crossing the Sea of Galilee. Arabic uses abhara/aqlaa (أَبْحَرَ/أَقْلَعَ, 'to set sail'), Hebrew hiflig (הִפְלִיג, 'to sail'), Korean chulhang-hada (출항하다, 'to depart port'), Hindi chalna (चलना, 'to depart/go'), Spanish zarpar ('to weigh anchor/set sail'), French mettre en mer ('to put to sea'). The middle/passive voice (anekhthesan, anakhthentes) is standard for this nautical sense in Hellenistic Greek.

To lead or conduct someone physically upward or to a higher place, or to bring before an authority. Jesus was 'led up' into the wilderness to be tempted (Matt 4:1), the infant Jesus was 'brought up' to the temple in Jerusalem (Luke 2:22), the devil 'led him up' to show kingdoms (Luke 4:5), Paul was 'brought up' from the dungeon (Acts 9:39), Herod intended 'to bring up' Peter before the people (Acts 12:4), and the Philippian jailer 'brought them up' into his house (Acts 16:34). Arabic uses sa'ida bihi (صَعِدَ بِهِ, 'went up with him') and Hebrew he'elu (הֶעֱלוּ, 'they brought up'). Korean uses deryeo-gada (데려가다, 'to take/lead someone'), Spanish llevar/subir ('to carry/bring up'). The literal spatial 'upward movement' with a person as object distinguishes this from the nautical sense.

labelChirho: bring up from the dead, raise
descriptionChirho: To bring up from the realm of the dead, a theological extension of the spatial 'lead up' sense applied to resurrection. In Rom 10:7, Paul asks 'Who will descend into the abyss? (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).' In Heb 13:20, God is praised as the one who 'brought up from the dead our Lord Jesus, the great shepherd of the sheep.' Arabic uses as'ada (أَصْعَدَ, 'to bring up'), German hinauffuehren ('to lead up'), Korean ikkeul-eo ollishin (이끌어 올리신, 'raised up'). The Hebrew in Heb 13:20 uses me'im (מֵעִים), contextually 'from among (the dead).' This sense is a metaphorical/theological specialization of the physical 'bring up' sense, specifically reserved for resurrection contexts.

To bring something up as a sacrificial offering, presenting it to God. In Acts 7:41, Stephen recounts that the Israelites 'offered up' (anegagon) a sacrifice to the golden calf in the wilderness. Arabic uses qaddamu (قَدَّمُوا, 'they presented/offered'), Hebrew he'elu (הֶעֱלוּ, 'they brought up,' the standard OT sacrificial term for offering on an altar), Korean ollida (올렸다, 'raised/offered'), Spanish ofrecieron ('they offered'). Hindi uses charhaya (चढ़ाया, 'offered up'). This cultic-sacrificial use connects to the literal 'bring up' (onto an altar) but is semantically specialized to the domain of worship and sacrifice.
